passage: I'm Darshan, and my little brother Suraj is five. At our cousin's birthday he spent the first half hour behind Amma's legs, holding her dupatta. When Mami asked his name, he whispered it into Amma's side. An uncle snapped, "Say hello properly, don't be like that," and Suraj went stiff, eyes down. Amma just said, "He'll come when he's ready." He watched musical chairs for three rounds. He let go and stood near the edge. In the fourth round he was in it, laughing. I can't know what he was thinking, but I think he wanted to play all along.

qa.q: Where did Suraj spend the first half hour?
qa.a: Behind Amma's legs, holding her dupatta.

qa.q: What does Darshan think Suraj wanted all along?
qa.a: Darshan thinks Suraj wanted to play all along, even while hiding and watching.

qa.q: Which response helped Suraj more, the uncle's or Amma's, and why?
qa.a: Amma's; letting him come when ready gave him time, while the uncle's push made him freeze.

qa.q: How might the uncle see Suraj after the fourth round?
qa.a: He may realise Suraj wasn't being rude, just needing time, since he ended up laughing in the game.

grounding: An older brother watches a five-year-old hide at a party, freeze when pushed to say hello, and join only after watching.

passage:

Friday. Lakshmi took the spade. By the end of the morning she was filling buckets beside the same boy, humming. At home she told her father, "He's my friend. His name is Omar."

qa.a: He offered her a spade.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi watching the boy after shaking her head suggest?

qa.q: How might Omar feel when Lakshmi finally takes the spade?

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage:
All through Class 5, I watched the lane cricket from our gate. I knew every player's name and who bowled fast. I wanted to play so badly that I practised bowling against our wall at night. But I never asked. I was sure I'd say something stupid, or they'd say no, and then I'd have to walk past them every day. Then Vijay, who lived two houses down, came to the gate one evening. "You're the one who bowls against the wall, na? We need a bowler." I followed, heart thudding. My first ball was a wide. Nobody laughed. My third ball took a wicket. Now I'm in Class 6. I still get nervous sometimes, but I ask. "Can I bat next?" It gets easier every time.
Ramesh

qa.q: Where did Ramesh practise bowling at night?
qa.a: Against the wall at home, at night.

qa.q: What worried Ramesh about asking to play?
qa.a: Ramesh was sure of saying something stupid or being refused, and then having to walk past the players every day.

qa.q: What turning point came when Vijay came to the gate?
qa.a: Vijay invited Ramesh as a needed bowler, a friendly bridge; after that, with practice, asking got easier.

qa.q: How might the other players have seen Ramesh after the wicket?
qa.a: They may have seen a useful new bowler, not the quiet kid at the gate.

grounding: A child who longed to join lane cricket but waited to be invited remembers how a neighbour's invitation and practice eased the shyness.

passage:
At every family function, someone would say, "Kashish is the shy one," before I'd even opened my mouth. After a while I stopped trying. If everyone already knew I was shy, what was the point? Then Shalini Ma'am came to teach us in Class 5. She never called me shy, not once. When I read one line aloud in a tiny voice, she said, "You read that line in front of thirty people. That was brave." The next week I read two lines. At Diwali, when Chachi said, "Oh, our shy Kashish," I heard myself say, "I read two lines in class this week." Chachi blinked. I don't think I'm "the shy one" anymore. I'm someone who gets braver in small steps.
Kashish

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am say after Kashish read one line?
qa.a: "You read that line in front of thirty people. That was brave."

qa.q: Why did Kashish stop trying at family functions?
qa.a: Kashish had come to believe being shy was fixed, so trying felt pointless.

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am do instead of labelling, and what changed?
qa.a: She praised the small brave step, and the next week Kashish read two lines.

qa.q: How might Chachi feel when Kashish answers with the two lines?
qa.a: She seemed surprised, blinking, and may start to see Kashish differently.

grounding: A child labelled shy by relatives starts to believe it, until a teacher praises small brave steps instead.

passage:
Note for Sunaina's parents, from Kavitha, class teacher
When I asked Sunaina to take the register to the office today, she said, "I can't, I'm shy. Everyone says so." She is eight, and she already believes it is who she is. At the parents' evening I noticed she was introduced to me the same way. I'd like to suggest we stop using the word, at school and at home. Instead, let's notice small brave steps. Today she carried the register with a friend and said "good morning" to the office staff in a whisper. I told her, "You did something new today." She smiled all through lunch. Tomorrow she will try it on her own.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say when asked to take the register?
qa.a: "I can't, I'm shy. Everyone says so."

qa.q: What does Sunaina's reply show she believes about herself?
qa.a: She believes shyness is who she is, not something that can change.

qa.q: What change does Kavitha suggest to Sunaina's parents?
qa.a: To stop using the word "shy" and to notice small brave steps instead.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after hearing "You did something new today"?
qa.a: She felt proud and capable; she smiled all through lunch.

grounding: A teacher sees an eight-year-old who has taken on the shy label and asks her parents to drop it and praise small brave steps.

passage:

I'm in 11B. You probably don't know me, which is sort of the problem. I haven't answered a question in class this year, even when I know the answer. My mum doesn't know how bad it is. Could I come and see you on Thursday in the free period? I'm scared even sending this.

passage:
Himani, you asked what happens when I have to speak in class. Here's the inside view. My heart starts pounding before my name is even called. My face goes hot; I can feel it turning red, which makes it redder. Then my mind goes blank, even if I studied. Afterwards I replay every second on the bus home: the pause, the wobble, the one kid who smirked. For months I just avoided it. I'd take the zero for oral work and feel so relieved. But the fear got bigger, not smaller. So with the counsellor I've made a ladder: first, reading one line to her; then answering one yes-or-no question in class; then, one day, the whole presentation. Yesterday I did step two.
Kishore

qa.a: Kishore did step two.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after taking the zero for oral work?
qa.a: So relieved at the time, though the fear kept getting bigger.

qa.q: What plan did Kishore make with the counsellor, and why does it help?
qa.a: A ladder of small steps, from reading one line to the whole presentation, so the fear shrinks through gentle practice instead of avoidance.

qa.q: What might Himani understand after hearing the inside view?
qa.a: Himani may realise that Kishore's silence in class comes from a pounding heart and a blank mind, not from not studying.

grounding: A teenager describes a racing heart, blushing and a blank mind before speaking, the relief and cost of avoiding, and a gentle step-by-step plan with a counsellor.

passage:
I sit next to Madhav in Hindi class, so I see it up close. When the teacher says, "Madhav, read the next paragraph," his ears go red first, then his neck. His hand grips the book so tight the page crinkles. He reads the first line, stops, and stares at the words as if they've turned into another language. He sits down, and for the rest of the period he doesn't look up. Last month he stopped coming on Fridays, when we have recitation. I don't know what he's thinking; he never says. But this week the teacher started letting him read sitting down, one line, then two. On Friday he came. He read four lines. His ears were still red. He finished anyway.
Yusuf

passage: The exchange students' bus was forty minutes late, so the teachers squeezed the welcome into ten rushed minutes: everyone would stand up and introduce themselves, one by one, in English. "Party on the terrace tonight, forty people. You're coming," Siddharth said.
